ann.l: This large polymorphonuclear neutrophil contains dozens of tiny, pink-magenta, paired cocci (diplococci) within its cytoplasm. Seeing these intracellular organisms in a purulent specimen is highly characteristic of Neisseria gonorrhoeae.

Another neutrophil shows the same intracellular pink-magenta diplococci. The pink color indicates they are gram-negative, having a thin peptidoglycan layer that does not retain the crystal violet stain during decolorization.

A few diplococci lie outside the cells in the extracellular space. While most gonococci are intracellular during acute infection, some free organisms are commonly observed in the background of the smear.

The field is crowded with numerous uninfected, multilobed neutrophils. Neisseria gonorrhoeae infection triggers a robust, purulent inflammatory response, resulting in an abundance of polymorphonuclear leukocytes in the discharge.

findings: Neutrophil, center left: a polymorphonuclear cell with a pink lobed nucleus holds dozens of tiny paired cocci in its cytoplasm. Seeing the organisms inside the white cell is the pattern typical of gonococci in pus.

Neutrophil, upper center: a second white cell carries the same pink-magenta pairs, so intracellular organisms recur across the smear. The pink color means a thin peptidoglycan wall that lost the crystal violet at decolorization, so the bacteria are gram-negative.

Free pair: a few diplococci lie outside the cells, for example just below the center-left neutrophil. Most gonococci sit inside neutrophils in acute infection, but some are found free in the background.

Surrounding neutrophils: the many segmented, multilobed cells around the infected ones fill the field because gonococci provoke a purulent exudate, so a Gram stain of discharge shows abundant polymorphonuclear cells besides the bacteria.
